content: 1. A field trial published in Nature in 2019 by Minassian AM, Silk SE, Barrett JR, Nielsen CM, Miura K, Diouf A, et al., demonstrated reduced blood-stage malaria growth and identified immune correlates in humans following RH5 vaccination. 2. Draper SJ, Angov E, Horii T, Miller LH, Srinivasan P, Theisen M, et al., in a 2015 Vaccine publication, reviewed recent advances in recombinant protein-based malaria vaccines, highlighting their potential and challenges. 3. The development of adjuvants for vaccines, as well as for autoimmune and allergic diseases, was discussed in a 2020 report from the Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer program in Washington, DC. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) released guidelines in 2014 on the quality, safety, and efficacy of recombinant malaria vaccines targeting the pre-erythrocytic and blood stages of Plasmodium falciparum (Annex 3, TRS No. 980). 5. WHO's preferred product characteristics (PPC) for malaria vaccines were outlined in a 2014 document, emphasizing the need for vaccines to meet specific safety and efficacy standards. 6. A 2022 WHO position paper on malaria vaccines, published in the Weekly Epidemiological Record, provided updated recommendations and insights into the use of RTS,S/AS01 in endemic regions. 7. Tinto H, Otieno W, Gesase S, Sorgho H, Otieno L, Liheluka E, et al., in a 2019 Lancet Infectious Diseases study, reported on the long-term incidence of severe malaria in children and infants following RTS,S/AS01 vaccination in Africa, based on a three-year extension of a phase 3 trial. 8. Milligan P and Moore K presented an unpublished statistical report in 2021 on the results of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine pilot evaluation, 24 months after its introduction. 9. Penny MA, Galactionova K, Tarantino M, Tanner M, and Smith TA, in a 2015 BMC Medicine article, used phase III data and simulation models to predict the public health impact of RTS,S in malaria-endemic African countries. 10. Vekemans J, Guerra Y, Lievens M, Benns S, Lapierre D, Leach A, et al., conducted a pooled analysis of safety data from pediatric phase II RTS,S/AS malaria vaccine trials, published in Human Vaccines in 2011. 11. Asante KP, Abdulla S, Agnandji S, Lyimo J, Vekemans J, Soulanoudjinga S, et al., in a 2011 Lancet Infectious Diseases study, evaluated the safety and efficacy of the RTS,S/AS01E malaria vaccine when co-administered with expanded immunization program vaccines. 12. Agnandji ST, Asante KP, Lyimo J, Vekemans J, Soulanoudjinga SS, Owusu R, et al., in a 2010 Journal of Infectious Diseases article, assessed the safety and immunogenicity of RTS,S/AS01E when integrated into routine immunization schedules. 13. Talaat KR, Ellis RD, Hurd J, Hentrich A, Gabriel E, Hynes NA, et al., in a 2016 PloS One study, investigated the safety and immunogenicity of PfS25-EPA/Alhydrogel®, a transmission-blocking vaccine against Plasmodium falciparum, in malaria-naïve adults. 14. Guimarães LE, Baker B, Perricone C, and Shoenfeld Y, in a 2015 Pharmacological Research article, explored the relationship between vaccines, adjuvants, and autoimmunity, discussing potential mechanisms and implications. 15. The WHO published an operations manual in 2009 on malaria case management, providing practical guidance for healthcare providers in endemic regions. 16. In 2008, the WHO released a chart booklet for the integrated management of childhood illnesses in high HIV settings, emphasizing the importance of tailored approaches. 17. A 2011 WHO operational manual outlined strategies for achieving universal access to malaria diagnostic testing, highlighting the importance of accurate and timely diagnosis. 18. A 1988 WHO memorandum discussed advancements in malaria diagnosis, emphasizing the need for improved diagnostic tools and techniques. 19. The WHO's 2016 Malaria Microscopy Quality Assurance Manual (version 2) provided guidelines for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of malaria microscopy. 20. Kawamoto F and Billingsley PF, in a 1992 Parasitology Today article, described a rapid malaria diagnostic method using fluorescence microscopy. 21. The WHO's 2003 publication, Malaria Diagnosis: New Perspectives, reviewed emerging diagnostic technologies and their potential impact on malaria control. 22. A 2003 WHO meeting report, Malaria Rapid Diagnosis: Making It Work, summarized discussions on the implementation and optimization of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). 23. The WHO's 2004 report on the use of RDTs emphasized their role in improving malaria diagnosis and treatment in resource-limited settings. 24. A 2009 WHO manual provided guidance on the transportation, storage, and handling of malaria RDTs in health clinics, ensuring their effectiveness and reliability. 25. The WHO's 2018 report on malaria RDT performance presented results from product testing (Round 8), evaluating the accuracy and reliability of various RDTs. 26. A 2017 WHO publication addressed the implications of false-negative RDT results due to P. falciparum HRP2/3 gene deletions, highlighting the need for alternative diagnostic strategies. 27. Abba K, Deeks JJ, Olliaro P, Naing CM, Jackson SM, Takwoingi Y, et al., in a 2011 Cochrane Review, evaluated the effectiveness of RDTs for diagnosing uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in endemic countries. 28. Thiam S, Thior M, Faye B, Ndiop M, Diouf ML, Diouf MB, et al., in a 2011 PloS One study, reported a significant reduction in antimalarial drug consumption in Senegal following the nationwide introduction of RDTs. 29. Voller A, in a chapter from Malaria: Principles and Practice of Malariology (1988), discussed the immunodiagnosis of malaria, detailing the use of serological methods. 30. Bates I, Iboro J, and Barnish G, in a 2003 publication, highlighted challenges in monitoring the impact of malaria interventions using diagnostics, emphasizing the need for robust evaluation frameworks.
